title: the tattoo that's really about today
hookLine: a skull, an hourglass, a wilting rose: a death reminder that's really about living

lines: A SKULL. AN HOURGLASS. A ROSE.
cards: A skull on a forearm. An hourglass. A wilting rose with two Latin words underneath.
Memento mori tattoos are everywhere, and they can look a little goth. The idea behind them is older and warmer than the ink suggests.
A Roman emperor practiced it in a private notebook, and his version ends somewhere you might not expect. First, a guess.

teach.b: Memento mori is Latin: remember that you will die. It sounds grim. It was meant as the opposite.
Marcus Aurelius, emperor of Rome, kept a notebook of reminders to himself, now called the Meditations, and he came back to death again and again.

In one old translation: "Do not act as if thou wert going to live ten thousand years. Death hangs over thee. While thou livest, while it is in thy power, be good." Listen to where it lands. Not on fear.
On be good, while you can. One honest note: Marcus wrote in Greek. The Latin phrase is better known from later Christian art, the skulls and hourglasses tucked into old paintings.
And no single school owns the idea. Early Buddhist texts teach mindfulness of death as a regular practice, and a psalm asks to be taught to number our days. Here's the napkin math that makes it land.
Eighty years is a little over four thousand weeks. Put the end in view, and the middle comes clear: the call, the apology, the trip stop waiting for next month.

how: Reflecting on death is an old practice: Stoics reminded themselves of it in their notebooks and letters, Buddhists practice maranasati (mindfulness of death), and Christian art used the memento mori, a skull or an hourglass, as a reminder.

practice: Three breaths with the bell. On the first, notice that this breath is one of a limited number: not a threat, just a fact. On the second, let one thing come to mind that you keep saving for next month.
On the third, let it come a little closer.
